Random forest for regression and probabilities

Source: R/rf.R
rfor.Rd

Grows a random forest (Breiman 2001) on x and y and returns its mean prediction at the rows of newx and its out-of-bag prediction at each row of x. Each tree is grown on a bag of rows drawn from x, as deep as minnode allows, choosing at each node the best of mtry columns drawn at random by the reduction in the sum of squares; for a 0/1 outcome this is the Gini split, and the forest's mean is a probability, as in a probability forest of 'ranger'.

Usage

rfor(
  x,
  y,
  newx = x,
  ntree = 500,
  mtry = NULL,
  minnode = 5,
  frac = 1,
  repl = TRUE,
  hon = FALSE,
  imb = 0,
  seed = 1
)

Arguments

x

The predictors: a numeric matrix with at least two rows, no missing values.

y

The outcome: one finite number per row of x; 0 or 1 for a probability.

newx

The rows to predict: a numeric matrix with the columns of x.

ntree

The number of trees: one whole number, at least 1.

mtry

The columns tried at each split: NULL for min(ceiling( sqrt(p) + 20), p), p the number of columns (the rule of 'grf'), or a whole number from 1 to the number of columns.

minnode

Nodes of at most this many rows are not split: one whole number, at least 1 (5 is the default of 'ranger' for regression, 10 for probabilities).

frac

The size of each bag as a share of the rows of x: above 0, at most 1.

repl

TRUE to draw bags with replacement, FALSE without.

hon

TRUE for honest trees (Wager and Athey 2018): each bag is shuffled, its first half places the splits and its second half sets the leaf means (a leaf without such rows takes the mean of its deepest ancestor that has some). Needs bags of at least two rows.

imb

Each child of a split must hold at least this share of its node's rows (and one row): one number from 0 to below 0.5 ('grf' uses 0.05).

seed

The seed of the draws: one number, at least 0. The same seed and data give the same forest.

Value

A list: pred, the predictions at the rows of newx, and oob, the out-of-bag prediction at each row of x (NaN for a row that every tree's bag holds).

Details

Each column is cut once, at its own order statistics, into at most 256 bins: every split between neighbouring values when a column has at most 256 distinct values (as an exact search finds), and splits at 255 quantiles otherwise. A node's best split then comes from one pass over its rows, and the forest depends on each column only through the order of its values: a strictly increasing transform of a column changes nothing. The forest is not bit-for-bit that of 'ranger' (it draws its own random numbers and uses quantile bins on columns of many values); tests compare their errors on known functions instead.

Defaults

The defaults were chosen by test error against the true function over four data-generating functions (a sparse linear one, Friedman's, a step-and-curve one and a probability), p = 20 and 200, ten seeds each (dev/rftune.R). Like for like (the same trees, mtry, node size, half-samples without replacement, imb = 0.05, honest or not), rfor() and 'grf' have test errors within 1 to 3 per cent of each other, inside two standard errors in almost every cell. The one setting that mattered was mtry: the rule of 'grf' lowers the error against the square root of p by 30 to 50 per cent on the sparse and step functions, so it is the default. Bags of all rows drawn with replacement gave the lowest error with that mtry in most cells; honest trees and half-samples raised the error of the predictions (honesty serves inference, not prediction), so both are options, off by default. Nodes of 5 rows are left unsplit, as both packages do.

References

Breiman, L. (2001). Random forests. Machine Learning, 45(1), 5-32. doi:10.1023/A:1010933404324

Wager, S. and Athey, S. (2018). Estimation and inference of heterogeneous treatment effects using random forests. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 113(523), 1228-1242. doi:10.1080/01621459.2017.1319839

Examples

set.seed(1)
x <- matrix(rnorm(400 * 4), 400)
y <- sin(2 * x[, 1]) + x[, 2] + rnorm(400, sd = 0.3)
f <- rfor(x, y, ntree = 100)
mean((f$oob - y)^2)
#> [1] 0.184494
